extracted.intended_audience: EEOC staff, employment-law practitioners, policymakers, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: A law-review Comment arguing that the EEOC should issue clear guidance declaring discrimination based on sexual orientation to be prohibited under Title VII via sex stereotyping and Macy’s "per se because of sex" theory, and explaining why prompt guidance is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex stereotyping theory (Hopkins approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination because an individual transgresses gender norms (fails to conform to sex stereotypes) is prohibited under Title VII — e.g., a woman punished for acting 'masculinely' violates sex stereotyping precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comment explains that when employers act against individuals for violating gender norms (for example, expecting men to be attracted only to women), that action is sex stereotyping. It provides doctrinal citations (Hopkins v. Price Waterhouse) and explanatory examples (a gay woman discriminated against for acting masculinely) to show sexual orientation discrimination fits within this theory and thus should be treated as impermissible under Title VII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macy’s "per se because of sex" theory applied to sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Macy, discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is always 'because of sex' because sexual orientation necessarily involves the gender of the person one is attracted to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comment argues that sexual orientation inherently has 'gender on the brain' — e.g., hypothetical Situation A/B (Pat attracted to Beth) demonstrates that the employer’s differing treatment turns on Pat’s gender as well as sexual orientation. Therefore, Macy’s reasoning that certain discrimination is per se because of sex should automatically encompass sexual-orientation discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of the conduct controls coverage under Title VII
rubrics_metrics.description: How courts characterize the discriminatory behavior (sex stereotyping/gender-based difference vs. equal treatment of men and women for same conduct) affects whether Title VII applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comment notes courts may (a) characterize discrimination as men and women being treated equally for being attracted to the same sex (thus not sex-based), (b) characterize conduct as a failure to conform to gender norms (sex stereotyping), or (c) treat the negative characteristic as "attraction to the same sex regardless of gender." Because characterization is dispositive, EEOC guidance must explicitly instruct on proper characterization and rebut common restrictive characterizations used by courts (citing DeSantis, Dillon, and other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: EEOC guidance must be clear and prompt
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission should promptly issue clear guidance stating that discrimination based on sexual orientation always provides a basis for a cognizable Title VII claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons for prompt guidance are given: (1) Macy could be interpreted in ways that do not include sexual orientation unless clarified, and (2) the EEOC’s composition and slow appellate processes mean a future Commission or delay could allow contrary, restrictive interpretations to gain force. The Comment urges issuance of guidance to avoid these risks and to ensure uniform treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance should address precedent and persuasiveness (deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: EEOC guidance is persuasive authority that courts may rely upon (Skidmore-level deference), and guidance can shape future judicial decisions even if not binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comment emphasizes that EEOC decisions and guidance are 'often persuasive in court decisions' and receive some deference (Skidmore), so explicit agency guidance extending Macy to sexual orientation would have significant practical impact despite not being Chevron-level substantive regulation. The guidance should therefore marshal precedent, agency decisions, and reasoning to maximize persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance must confront contrary federal precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any EEOC guidance should explicitly address and rebut appellate decisions that have refused to extend Title VII to sexual-orientation discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comment cites examples of federal appellate authority (e.g., Vickers v. Fairfield Med. Ctr., Dawson v. Bumble & Bumble, DeSantis v. Pac. Tel. & Tel. Co.) that have distinguished or excluded sexual-orientation claims; it argues the EEOC must acknowledge these rulings and explain why Macy/Hopkins reasoning nonetheless requires coverage for LGB people, to prevent those precedents from undermining a uniform interpretation.
